205.1: I shall describe the Bhismapaheaka, that is the foremost among the vows and that which yields everything. It should be done on the eleventh day in the bright fortnight in k&rttika.
205.2: (The observer of the vow) should bathe thrice (daily) for five days and satisfy gods and manes with five kinds of grains and sesamum. He should worship lord Hari silently.
205.3: Having bathed the deity with the five things got from a cow and with the five sweet things, sandal paste should be be¬ smeared and guggulu should be burnt along with ghee.
205.4: A lamp should be offered. Food offering should be made day and night. He should then repeat (the syllable) "Om obei¬ sance to Vasudeva" one hundred and eight times.
205.5: The performer of the vow should then make oblations of sesamum and rice dipped in ghee with the sacred syllable of six letters along with the word 'oblations.'
205.6: After having practised the (Bhismapancaka)Bhlsma, reach¬ ed lord Hari. That is why (it is known as) Bhismapancaka. One should worship lord Brahma and fast while practising the vow.

211.3: By giving hundred cows one becomes free from the ocean of hells. By giving a weaned calf one stays in comfort in the heaven.

211.8: One who makes a gift of cloth would get longevity,
211.11: By giving fire and firewood (for travellers) on the way, one would get radiance etc. and would be served in the (celes- tial)vehicle in heaven by the celestials, gandharvas and women.

225.1: He should not be given (an opportunity) to associate with angry, greedy and dishonoured persons. If not able to inculcate virtue (in the prince, the king) should bind him with pleasures.
225.2: An obedient prince should be engaged in all posts of authority. The king should avoid hunting, drinking and dice (playing) that destroys the kingdom.
225.3: One should avoid passion, anger,' haughtiness, pride.
225.4: Then (he) should subjugate his external enemies. The external enemies are of three kinds — those belonging to the same clan, those having enmity from the period of the ances¬ tors and those who have enmity on account of some particular reason. Among these three each preceding one is greater than the succeeding one.
225.5: O Fortunate one! Friends are of three kinds — friend of the father and grandfather, feudatory under the enemy and artificial.
225.6: The gods and all brahmins should always be worshipp¬ ed and gifts should be given to them (brahmins). Gift made to a brahmin (would be) imperishable and the treasury cannot be destroyed by any of these.
225.7: Not retreating in the battle, protecting the subjects and giving gifts to the brahmins are the supreme good for a king.
225.8: (The king) should likewise arrange for the welfare and livelihood of the poor, destitute and old people, widows and women whose husbands have gone abroad.

227.1: The king should levy a fine of one suvarna for one who promises (to give something) and does not give. One who accepts payment and does not do the work should be levied a fine of eight krsrtalas.
227.2: One who accuses his mother or father or elder brother or father-in-law or the preceptor should be levied a fine of one hundred (panas). (The same punishment should be levied) for obstructing the pathway of the preceptor.
227.3: One of a lower caste should without enquiry be severed
227.4: The killers of a cow, elephant, horse or camel should have their legs and hands cut off. One who would make a tree barren deserves the fine of a suiarna.
227.5: The organ with which one would steal from others should be removed by the king for the sake of discipline.
227.6: One who seizes the house or field (belonging to another, ) one who copulates with another's wife, one who is an incendiary and one who administers poison should be killed. So also in the case of one who attacks with a drawn weapon.
227.7: Those who have been employed to do certain work if do not do the work of their employers, the king should make those shameless, cruel-minded to be penniless.
227.8: Likewise the king should banish the minister or justice after having taken the entire (property) for doing the work of another (king).
227.9: If one violates the bed of the preceptor, (mark of) female generative organ should be made (on the forehead), a pot of wine in case of drinking of wine, a dog in case of stealing and the head of a person in the case of killing a brahmin.

237.3: The water of libation (should be done) in this way in the death of the maternal grand-father, and the preceptor.The water of libation is optional in (the case of) the death of the girl friend, sister's son, father-in-law and priest.

237.8: If a pollution due to death occurs while there is pollu¬ tion due to birth and vice-versa, the pollution is based on that of death only and not on that of birth.
237.9: If death occurs at the end of another death, there is purification after the end of first pollution. The greater one always affects the lighter one. But the lighter one never affects the greater one.
237.10: If the pollution due to death or birth occurs in the mid¬ night when there is already a pollution due to death or birth, all would become pure with the remaining part of pollution. That is that part of the night added to two days.
237.11: If the pollution occurs in the morning, one becomes pure after three days. In both cases one should not eat food from that family.
237.12: One should refrain from making any gifts. If one hap¬ pened to die, he should do riies of atonement. There is no sin if it is done unknowingly in the former. Otherwise, it would be for a day for the one who dines.

237.14: Even after the death (of a person), the relatives would not be able to follow the dead person, The path of death is differ¬ ent for all others except the wife.

252.1: Great men hold that the five ways of casting a noose are: extending in a straight line, long, broad, horizontal and whirling.
252.2: The uses of a disc (are): cutting, piercing, felling, whirling and severing.
252.3: jMay you know that the uses of a spear are: slapping, thrashing, cleaving, frightening, incarcerating and, the sixth, striking down.
252.4: O Excellent Brahmin! It has been declared that an iron club (TOMARA) (is used) in striking the eyes, the arms (and) sides (of the enemy) and should be countered with an arrow of the defendent.
252.5: O Brahmin! The use of a mudgara{m3LCc) is for striking, cutting, pounding, causing deluge and killing *
252.6: The uses of a bhindipala (sling) are for sarfilranta, otf- rdnta and govisarga and sudurdhara (that is extremely unbearable). The same are the uses of a laguda (club).
252.7: O Excellent Brahmin! The uses of a mace (VAJRA) are for (striking) with the end, with the middle, turning back and commanding. The same (are the uses) of a paffiia (a kind of spear with sharp edge).
252.8: Taking away, cutting, killing, piercing, anointing, felling and snapping are indicated as the uses of a sword.
252.9: The functions of a sling are indicated to be frighten¬ ing, protecting, killing and helping a big fighting column. The same are the functions of a machine also.

253.1: The conduct of a person (rests) on the opinion of the people. The decree (depends) on the command of* the king. Since (a legal case) could be decided by the means such as the conciliation (and the like), they are said to be the four means.
253.2: (The term) debt (denotes that admitted) by a person as payable or that denied by him as not payable or that which is given as gift (to another).
253.3: One's own property placed out of trust (with another) without any doubt is said by wise men to be a trust that is a matter of dispute.
253.4: The place where the merchants and others collectively transact business (called) the active occupation is known to be a matter of dispute.
253.5: If one wants to take back that he has paid (to an¬ other), that is called the withdrawer of a gift and is known to be the matter of dispute.
253.6: If one sells the entrusted property of another or the lost (property of another) after having got it or having stolen it without the knowledge (of the owner), it is known to be selling of another's property.
253.7: After having sold the goods for money if (the goods) are not made over to the buyer, it is non-delivery o sold (arti¬ cles) and is a matter for dispute.
253.8: The dispute that arises in respect of the right over the land that has been determined by a bridge or a held or drawn boundaries is said to be that (dispute) arising from the land.
253.9: Where the marriage rite of men and women is declared that is named as the union of women and men and is a matter for dispute.
253.10: A rash act done by those haughty of their strength is said to be a crime and is declared as a matter for dispute.
253.11: 'Dius disputes are of eighteen kinds and there are one hundred divisions of these. These hundred divisions (of disputes) are stated to be due to difference in the acts of men.

254.1: One that inherits a property, as well as the wife of a deceased person that inherits the property should be made to pay the ( incurred) debt. The debt of a sonless owner of a pro¬ perty (should be paid) by the person that inherits the property.
254.2: The husbands of the women of the gopa (a guard), Saudika (a distiller and seller of spirituous liquors), SailUfa (an actor or dancer), rajaka (a washerman) or lySdha,(a hunter) (castes) should repay the loan incurred by them because their livelihood is dependent on them (those women).
254.3: The wife need not repay any other loan except that (incurred by her husband) with her consent, or that incurred jointly with her husband or that incurred by herself.
254.4: The son need not repay the debt incurred by the father by drinking or wenching or by way of the balance of fine inflicted by the court or by making improper gifts.
254.5: A loan should be- got by a member of the undivided family against the surety of the brothers, the husband and wife, the father or the son.
254.6: A surety.consists in being a witness, or in giving a guarantee (for the repayment of aidebt). When a property is pledged by a person that has no rigiit of possession, the sons of that mortgager should be liable to repay (the incurred loan).
254.7: A mortgse shall be forfeited if that is not redeemed by paying double the amount. (The right for redemption) would cease at the lapse of the period agreed upon at the time of the mortgage. But it would not cease if enjoyments of the proceeds have been ageed upon.

255.1: Those who are not suitable to be witnesses are women, old men, children, cheats, intoxicated, lunatics, injured, actors, heretics, men of the writer caste, those having defective sense organs, those that take food from degraded persons, relatives or friends or enemies (of the persons contesting the dispute) and thieves. All people arc deemed to be witnesses in cases of thefts, violence and rashness. A virtuous man accepted by both the parties may be a witness. A person that refuses to answer the questions relating to a loan in which (interest) at the rate of ten per cent (has been allowed) should be made by the king to pay the full amount (together with interest) within fortysix days. The vilest person that does not depose the facts even though he is aware of them, is (considered) as equivalent to the sins of false witnesses and is also liable for similar punishment.
255.2: These are the five obligaUons that a person has to discharge daily-— the act of the religious instruction, offering water to the manes, oblations for the gods, oblations to the goblins and entertaining die guests.
255.3: The word Jdti denotes the castes in general mid the word vma denotes the four principal castes.
255.4: A deed that has beeh written in the handwriting of the mortgager is valid ' even without the attestation by the witnesses, except in (cases) where undue compulsion had been made.
255.5: The debt mentioned in a deed has to be discharged by the three men (the debtor, the son or grandson). A mort¬ gage remains in force until the pledge is not redeemed.
255.6: A new deed has to be written when the old one has been taken abroad or the original writing has len forged or lost or erased or seized or torn or mutilated or burnt.
255.7: (The accused) that has bathed together with the dress and observed fast should be called up and made to carry all the. ordeals in the presence of the king and brahmins.
255.8: (The accused) that is resorting to the balance is weighed by those conversant with balances. After the balance comes to rest, line is drawn and (the accused) is taken off.
255.10: (One should say as below in the water ordeal): "You are the mostholy among the holy. O Purifier! You purify the accused. O Varunia! (You) protect me with the truth.'* Having addressed (the water) thus, one should enter the water holding onto the thighs of a man standing in water upto his navel. His innocence would be established, if one bringing back an arrow simultaneously discharged, finds him fully dived (into the water).

256.1: After having given a little (of the share) to the wealthy that does not wish to have (the share then), the division (should be made afterwards). Unequal divisions made by the father (should be held as) legal.
256.2: The sons should equally divide (among themselves) the liabilities of their father afterwards. The outstanding debts of the mother (should be borne by) the daughters, if they had no progeny.
256.3: That which one has earned (by his effort) without the destruction of the paternal property, (that acquired) from friends (as a gift) and through marriage, cannot be claimed by the co-partencrs (for a share).
256.4: The benefits of a common property should be divided equally. The sons of different fathers (forming an undivided family) should take their shares according to (the shares of) their fathers.
256.5: Both the father and the son would be entitled to equal shares in the property or wealth of the land acquired by the grand-father.
256.6: One should not give to the co-parceners an ancestral property that was lost and recovered by him, as well as that acquired by (his own) skill.
256.7: The property that has been given to one by his parents would be his own. But the mother also would have an equal share in the property that has been divided by the grand¬ father.
256.8: The property that has been wrongly taken possession of by somebody and divided should again be equally divided. That is the practice.
256.9: A son got by one not having a son by niyoga}- through another's wife inherits the properties of both the parents. He ( is allowed) by the codes of law to do the obsequies ( of his father).
256.10: A son born to one through liis lawful wife (is called) aurasa (legitimate). A daughter's son (is deemed) to be ranking
256.11: A son clandestinely begotten in the (paternal) House (of a woman) is known to be born in secret. A son born to a virgin (is known as) Artna and is held to be the son of the maternal grandfather (girl's father).
256.12: A son born (of a married woman by another), whether she had menstruated or not, (is known as) paunarbhava. A son given as adoption by his mother or father would be a dattaka (an adopted son).
256.13: A son sold by them (his original parents) is known as krita (bought). A son adopted without the consent of his parents would be (known as) artificial. A son offering himself (as a son) to another is (known as) dattdtman (one that offers himself). A son in the womb (at the time of his mother's marriage) is known as sahodaja (son of a woman pregnant at marriage).
256.14: A son deserted (by his father) and becoming a filial (of another) is known as apaviddha (abandoned). (All these) are eligible to offer cakes (at the obsequies) and to inherit their shares. Among these, the subsequent ones (are eligible) if the preceding ones do not exist.
256.15: One of the twelve kinds of sons allowed by the law for inheritance; the others being, attrasa, paunarthiaa, dattaka, krita, kftrma, sahadja, iat/iddha, jSdkatpama, kdnlna, svqyaiHdatta and iaudra. (See Mam IX,, 138-60. 166-80)
256.16: The preceptor, the good disciple, the fellow religious student of the same religious order are duly the heirs to the prop>erties of a vanaprastha (forester), ascetic and a religious student.
256.17: A coparcener and a brother may give to a coparcener or a brother that is born or may take away from a coparcener or a brother that is dead.
256.18: The coparcener not born of the same womb should not inherit the property of one not born of the same womb. A coparcener not born of the same womb should not inherit the property of one born of different mother.
256.19: The wives of men not having sons should be maintained if they follow pious paths. But those (wives) that are unchaste and infidels should be banished.
256.20: The wealth of a woman not having progeny (would belong) to the husband after her death (applicable to) all the four castes such as the brahmins etc. The daughters (would be the legal heirs) if they had delivered a child. Otherwise it would go to the father.
256.21: Property, gifts etc. made to a first wife upon marrying a second.
256.22: A husband need not return the wealth of his wife in the event of (it being spent to meet) a famine, relfgious obser¬ vance, illness or on account of imprisonment.
256.23: One should pay an amount of wealth to his second wife equal with what he has done to his first wife. If he has not given to the first wife already, he should pay a half now.

257.1: Four or eight or ten guards wearing (garland of) red flowers and red dress should be there in each village for laying the boundaries.
257.2: (Those that make a) false statement (relating to the boundaries of a field) should be punished with the madhyamasd- hasa. In the absence of men familiar with the fields or the marks of identification, the king himself should demarcate.
257.3: One cf three kinds of penalties or modes of punishment.
257.4: If one transgresses the boundary or encroaches into (another's) field or removes the boundary, that person is to be punished with the adhama or uttama or madhyama {sdhasa)?-
257.5: A minor encroachment should not be obstructed if it is for the sake of a bridge that benefits (all). (Similarly) one that encroaches another's field for a well occupying a little space and providing copious water (should not be obstructed).
257.6: One who does not cultivate or employ ( someone) to cultivate in a field that has been tilled should not be given the fruits of the cultivation and the field should be made over to another (for cultivation).
257.7: The owner of the field would get the same quantity of grains that has been destroyed (as above). The keeper (of the animal ) should be beaten and the owner of the cow should get the punishment already described.
257.8: The cows let loose by strong bulls, (the cow) that has delivered (a calf), the cow that has strayed and those that have tlie keeper should be freed (i.e. not to be punished). (So also cows) injured accidentally or by the king (should also not be punished).
257.9: Three kinds of fines of vnrying proportions.
257.10: The cowherd should return the cows in the evening as entrusted to him (in the morning). A paid servant is boimd to pay (the price of the animals) that were killed or lost (in his custody) by his negligence.
257.11: The pasture land should be set apart (at a place) according to the wish of ( the people of) the village or being beneficial to the land and the king. A brahmin may collect grass, fuel and flowers from any land as if it were his own.
257.12: The extent of the interspace between the village and the field should be one hundred dhanus while that between the market- town (and the field) should be two hundred (dflwuj) and that between the city (and the field should be) four hund¬ red (dhanus).
257.13: (A man) who has found out a lost and stolen (article) should cause the thief to be apprehended. But if there was a lapse of time and (was found), at a distant place, (the owner) should himself apprehend (the thief) and hand him over (to the authorities).
257.14: (The purcliaser) gets free after showing the seller (of a stolen property). The owner (would get) the property. The king (would get) the fine. The purchaser would get his money back from the seller.
257.15: Allowance should be made for wear and tear by way of addition or enjoyment (for an article). If it exceeds the limit, a five-fold fine (should be paid) to the king.
257.16: A man who recovers or takes back a stolen or lost article from another, without intimating the king should be fined (to pay) ninetysix panas.
257.17: A lost or stolen article recovered by the customs officers or sentinels (should be given) to the owner if it is less than a year (after its loss) and thereafter (it should be) with the king.
257.18: One should pay (as interest) four paas for a single hoofed animal, five for a slave, two for a buffalo, camel and cow and one fourth of that for a goat and sheep.
257.19: One may give away ( his possessions ), except his wife and son, for interest, without causing hardship to his own family members, if not objected to by any of them. If he docs not have the progeny, he may give all his possessions.
257.20: The acceptance (of a property) should be made public, especially of an immovable property. After having given the promised thing that is payable to one, one should not take it back.
257.21: A person who gives the seed, iron, vehicle, gem, woman, milch animal and a man should wait for ten, one, five, seven days, a month, three days and a fortnight respectively (for inte¬ rest).
257.22: A pupil who has completed his studies should stay for the stipulated period at the house of liis preceptor and has to serve him for the food got from him.
257.23: The king should allot |i frontal place to the •brahmins (in his city), provide for their livelihood by means of the three Vge/as and tell them, "May you adhere to your own duty".
257.24: Everyone should follow the words of those who preach for the welfare of the society. One who does the contrary should be made to pay the first {sdhasa) fine.
257.25: Those who think of public service should be learned in the scriptures and not greedy. (All) should follow the words of those who speak for the welfare of the society.
257.26: ■ The same rule ( holds good) in the case of guild of traders, assembly of interpreters of the scriptures and those professing other religions. The king has to maintain the separate entities of these and govern the former profession.
257.27: One who does not do a work after having received the wages (for the same) should pay double the amount ( as fine). (If the amount) has not been taken, one has to pay an equal amount (as fine). The supplementary grants (given to the servants) should be retained by them.
257.28: One who gains by trade, cattle or grains without obtaining the previous permission should be made to pay one tenth (of the gain as fine) by the king.
257.29: A carrier should restore to the owner, the article that he was carrying but was lost due to causes other than the govern¬ ment or accident. One who causes obstruction to a public carrier should pay double the amount of the wages.

258.1: A person (who mates) with a slave girl ora maid¬ servant held in captivity, though otherwise fit for cohabitation, should be fined fifty panas.
258.2: A person who adds or omits in copying the royal edict or one who releases a seducer should be fined the highest {sdhas).
258.3: The two eyes should be plucked out in the case of a person who acts hostile to the king or the nation. A SUdra living like a brahmin (should be) fined eight hundred {pams).
258.4: If one has been defeated in the proper way, thinks that he is unconquered, he should be defeated ( again) when he comes and should be punished (to pay) double the (amount of) fine.
258.5: A king who has fined a person unjustly should offer the amount to (lord) Varuna and pay thirty times (the amount) to the brahmins.
258.6: Piety, wealth, fame, esteem of mankind, favour, love of the suljjects and permanent residence in heaven, dispensing justice even as (people) watch are the seven qualities of a king.
258.7: Atimukta will also get the same fruit. The pdfald (flower) conveys one to the world of Visnu. One gets the world of Visnu with the karavlra (flowers). One becomes fortunate with japd (flowers).
258.8: One would reach the world of Visnu with the pdvanti, kubjaka and tagara (flowers). (One would reach) the world of Visnu with the karnikara. There would be destruction of sin with kurmfha.
258.9: One who has discontinued (doing) five sacrifices' (would suffer) in kutfala hell eating urine and blood. One who has eaten the forbidden food would take blood in the filthy hell.
258.10: One who afflicts others would be tormented in the hell tailapdka like sesamum. One who kills a person who has sought refuge would be cooked in the tailapdka.
258.11: One who withholds gifts at the sacrifice and who sells wine would be thrown into the hell nirucchvdsa. Similarly,
258.12: To be performed by a householder — brahmayajfta, pitryajtla, daiva- pitryajHa,, bhSlayajfla and nryajha respectively denoting teaching, libation to manes, oblation to gods, offering made to spirits and feeding guests.
258.13: The killer of an animal (would be thrown) into an alkaline lake. One who steals the land (would be placed) under a current as sharp as a razor. One who steals a cow or gold (would be thrown) into (the hell) ambarisa. One who cuts a tree (would be put) in (the hell) vajraSastraka.
258.14: One who steals wine would be put into (hell)
258.15: One who receives a bribe (would be tormented) in (the hell) durdhara. One who cohabits women taken captive (would suffer) in the hell (called) manjusa. One who censures scriptures (would be thrown) in the unstable hell loha.
258.16: One who cohabits others' wives (would enter) (the hell) idlmala (and embrace) glowing iron or stone. Similarly, a woman cohabiting many men would do.
258.17: I shall describe the Bhismapaheaka, that is the foremost among the vows and that which yields everything. It should be done on the eleventh day in the bright fortnight in k&rttika.
258.18: (The observer of the vow) should bathe thrice (daily) for five days and satisfy gods and manes with five kinds of grains and sesamum. He should worship lord Hari silently.
258.19: Having bathed the deity with the five things got from a cow and with the five sweet things, sandal paste should be be¬ smeared and guggulu should be burnt along with ghee.
258.20: A lamp should be offered. Food offering should be made day and night. He should then repeat (the syllable) "Om obei¬ sance to Vasudeva" one hundred and eight times.
258.21: The performer of the vow should then make oblations of sesamum and rice dipped in ghee with the sacred syllable of six letters along with the word 'oblations.'
258.22: After having practised the (Bhismapancaka)Bhlsma, reach¬ ed lord Hari. That is why (it is known as) Bhismapancaka. One should worship lord Brahma and fast while practising the vow.

One who is possessed by Vinayaka dreams as if he is. bathing in water excessively, sees shaven heads, rides the demons (in a dream) and as he goes thinks that he is being followed by others. 276.1: Rukmipi, Satyabhama, Satya, Nagnajiti, Gan- dhari, Lakfmapa, Mitravinda, Kalindi, Jbavati, Suiila, Madri, Kausalya, Vijaya, J&yh and others were the sixteen thousand wives (of Krfna) among whom Satyabhama served (Lord) Hari(Kr9na).
276.2: There were twelve battles between the celestials and the demons for the sake of their (legitimate) portions. The first (war of Visnu was in) the man-lion form. The second war (was) as a dwarf.
276.3: The battle (fought) as the boar (was) the next one. The fourth one was for the churning of the nectar. The sixth one was the battle involving all the celestial bodies for the sake of resuscitation.
276.4: (The seventh one was the destruction of) the three cities. (The eighth one was for) the destruction of (the demon) Andhaka. The ninth one (was) the killing of (the demon) Vrtra. The deadly (poison of) halahala was conquered (in the tenth one). (The demom) Kolahala (was subdued in the next one).
276.5: (The next one was) the form as the man-lion, the protector of the celestials in olden days, that pierced the chest of (the demon) Hiranyakafipu with his nails and made Prahlada the king.
276.6: In (the dispute between) the celestials and the demons, (the Lord) was bom of Kaiyapa and Aditi as a dwarf, deceived the powerful (demon) Bali and restored the kingdom to Indra.
276.7: The manifestation as a boar (was made by Lord Vifnu) and the demon Hiranyaksa was killed, protecting the celestials thus. He lifted up the earth that got submerged and was praised by the celestials.
276.8: (The mount) 'Mandara was made the churning rod, (the serpent) Vasuki as the string and (the ocean) was churned by the celestials and the demons. The ambrosia (that was obtained) was given to the celestials.

276.10: (The sages) Vivamitra, Vasistha, Atri and Brahma protected the celestials in the battle after warding off the demons that were having infatuation and hatred.

280.4: The fourth, ninth and fourteenth days of a lunar fcfftnight.
280.5: Those that arc pungent, bitter and astringent produce wind and destroy phlegm. Similarly those that are pungent, sour and saline are known to increase bile.
280.6: Those that are bitter, sweet and astringent destroy bile. This is not the effect of the taste but only of its chemical action.
280.7: O Susruta! Those that are stimulant and hot destroy phlegm and wind. Those that are cold destroy bile. They (the herbs) exert their influence according to their qualities.
280.8: The three (seasons) beginning with the rainy (are said to be) visargas. The three (seasons) beginning with winter and ending with summer (are) adana.
280.10: The characteristics of the disease due to the (derang¬ ed) wind are — pain in the bones, bitter taste in the mouth, parched state of feeling in the mouth, yawning and bristling of the pair.
280.11: Tlie characteristics of disease due to phlegm are languor, flow of water (from the mouth), heaviness (of the body), sweet taste in the mouth and longing for heat.
280.12: (Eating of) oil and hot food, anointing the body with oil and bathing and drinking of oil and the like would appease (deranged) wind. Clarified butter, milk, sugar and the rays of the moon and the like would counter (deranged) bile.
280.13: The oil of the three myrobalans together with honey and doing exercises etc. would remove (deranged) phlegm. Contemplation on (Lord) Visnu and His worship would appease all the diseases.

281.1: O One possessing powerful arms! The tastes such as sweet, sour and saline are stated to come from the moon. The tastes — bitter, astringent and pungent — arc (known to be) from fire.
281.2: The herbs have three flavours — bitter, sour and saline. The strength (of the herbs) is said to be of two kinds — hot and cold.
281.3: O Foremost among the brahmins! The effect of the herbs is indescribable. Those that are sweet, astringent and bitter are said to be having cold potency. The rest are stated to be hot.
281.4: The saline and sweet teistes would become sweet flavour. The sour things that are hot are also said to become so. The rest would have pungent flavour.
281.5: One has to determine the drugs that have got modified in their potency and flavour from their efficacy. Honey, although sweet, is said to be pungent in flavour.
281.6: (The herb) should be boiled with water, sixteen times its proportion, until it comes down to four times the proportion. This is the general rule for (preparing) a decoction wherever (something else) has not been stated.
281.7: The decoction that is clear and having little medicinal ingredient would be as above described. (The dosage) for pulverised drugs is stated to be an aka (a particular measure of weight equal to lrnAfas) and four palas (a particular weight) for the decoction. This measure is said to be middling. There is no hard and fast rule about the dosage. O Fortunate one! The measure of the dosage has to be decided according to the age, time, strength, digestive power, place, herb and disease.
281.8: One should eat the three myrobalans together with the rock-salt, that would give good complexion to a king. (One would get similar benefit by using) the juice of venison together with rock-salt or curd or small quantities of milk. One whose constitution is windy should eat (a food) that has either more juice or the same proportion of juice. It is said that massaging (the body) (should be done) in sum'mer. In winter it should be in equilibrium. It is known to be of middling type in the spring. The intense massaging in the summer is first done on the skin and then on the muscles, veins, blood and the body.

282.1: (It is better) to have thorny trees on the south near the house. A garden should be near the house. Blooming sesa> mum plants should be gathered and the trees should be planted after worshipping a brahmin and the moon. The five fixed asterisms sv&ti hasta, rohii, iravana and rnUla are commended for planting the trees.

283.1: A decoction of /a/t, two kinds of niid (turmeric) and vatsaka is commended for all types of infantile dysentery as well as defects due to mother's milk.
283.2: One should lick pulverised irngi, krsd and atibalS to¬ gether with honey. (Otherwise) ativifS alone would remove the cough, vomitting and fever of a child.
283.3: Vacd should be taken by children together with clari¬ fied butter, or with milk or with oil. The child should drink yasfikd or iadkha flower together with milk. This would improve speech, complexion, longevity, intellect and beauty of the child. Vacd, agniSikhd, vdsd, dried ginger, krfnd (long pepper), turmeric, yafi and rock salt should be given to a child in the morning for drinking. It would develop the memory.
283.4: (Similarly) filling the ear with the juice of garlic, ginger and Sigru (would remedy the bleeding of the ears). Extracts of ginger and nutmeg in oil would remove intestinal colic and also the diseases of the lipsk
283.5: The outer skin of the nutmeg, dry ginger, pepper, long pepper and turmeric would remove the urinary defects. A paste of mustard made into a decoction in milk dissolved in oil would remove toothache.
283.6: The coriander water, coconut, cow's urine, betelnut and dry ginger made into a decoction and used for gargling would remedy the defects in the tongue.
283.7: The juice of nirgwdikd with the paste of Idngali prepared in oil when inhaled would destroy gandamdld and galagada.
283.8: One should rub (the affected part of the skin) with the leaves of arkat potikd and snuhi together with cow's urine. (By this one would destroy) all the defects of the skin.
283.9: VSkucl and sesamum eaten for one year is a cure fcMr leprosy. Pathyd, bhall&taki and a lump of molasses in oil would also conquer leprosy,
283.10: One suffering from piles should drink buttermilk to¬ gether with the powders of yQthikd, vahniy turmeric, the three myrobalans and vyofa or should take abhayd with molasses.
283.11: One suffering from a urinary ailment should take a decoction of the (three) myrobalans, a variety of turmeric and via or the juice of the emblic myrobalan or the paste of turmeric with or without honey should be used.
283.12: A decoction of vdsd mixed with castor oil would remove acute gout. The drinking (of the juice) of long pepper, would cure enlarged spleens.
283.13: The essence of the bark of pathyd, Sigru, karahja and arka together with honey and rock salt would cure abscess as well as (help) ripening of the intestines.
283.14: Oil boiled with fySmS, turmeric, lodhra, padmaka utpalOy sandal and black pepper, and distilled in milk w'ould heal a wound.
283.15: Burnt ashes of the leaves of black holy basil and cotton, nutmeg, rock-salt and turmeric made into a paste and boiled in oil in a copper vessel would be a good remedy for ulcers.
283.16: Kumbhisdra mixed with milk should be heated in fire and applied on the wound. It could also be cured by sprinkling with the chops of coconut and ghee.
283.17: Dried ginger, ajamoda, rock-salt and bark of tamarind in equal proportions together with mustard in the same propor¬ tion should be drunk with butter-milk or hot water. It would cure dysentery.
283.18: One suffering from any type of colic should drink warm water saturated with rock-salt burnt in charcoal. Alternatively (one may take a mixture of) rock-salt, asafoetida, long pepper ad mustard in the same way.
283.19: Drinking of a decoction of pathydy gokfuray dusparfay rdjavfkfa and Hldbhit together with honey would remedy painful discharge of urine.
283.20: A decoction of bamboo bark and vanma would remove stone in the bladder. One who is suffering from elephantiasis should take the decoction of idkhofaka ttether with honey and milk.
283.21: Oil made with blackgram and the milk extracted from the bark of arka (as well as) rock-salt mixed with honey would be remedy for the diseases of leg. Clarified butter similarly (would cure) jalakukkutaja}
283.22: Powder of dried ginger, natron and asafoetida mixed with the juice of dried ginger boiled with ghee would remove sickness and this decoction is known to be efficacious in improving digestion.
283.23: A decoction of emblic myrobalan, snake-gourd and greengram together with clarified butter would cure dry spread¬ ing itch. Dry ginger, ddru and navd made into a decoction with milk together with the urine of a cow also (would remove swelling).
283.24: Decoction of dry ginger, pepper, long pepper, k?ara and the three myrobalans would remove swelling. (Similar effect is had by using) treacle, Signi and trivrt together with pulverised rock-salt.

288.1: I shall describe the essence of (science relating to) the management of horses and the treatment of their diseases. In order to achieve dharma, artha (virtue) and kama (enjoyment and prosperity) (a king) should acquire (good) horses. (The asterisms) aivini, Sravaa, hasta and the three uttaras {uttardsd4hay attaraphdlguni and uttarabhddrapada) are commended for the first ride on the horses. The early winter, winter and spring are commendable for riding the horses. The riding of the horses in the summer, autumn and rainy season is forbidden. One should not whip the horses severely or with other kinds of sticks or at an improper place. One who rides a horse* at a place abounding in nails, thorns and bones, on a nigged ground, on a sandy and muddy ground and spoilt by • pits and falls without knowing the temper (of the steed) and without the saddle would be carried away by the horse even as he is seated on its back.
288.2: The mystical letter formii the essential part of the mantra of a After having repeated (the above prayer) into the ears (of his steed) the rider should confuse the enemy, saddle the horse and ride (the horse). (This would give him) victory in the battle. Generally the defects in the horses are produced in their bodies. The excellent riders should convert them into good qualities with much effort. The good qualities that are due to the ability of the riders would appear as natural.
288.3: Other riders would destroy even the natural qualities. Some know the good qualities. Some others know their defects. One is fortunate who knows (the qualities as well as the defects in) a horse. A stupid one is he who does not know both. One who knows the means (of handling an emergent situation ), one who knows the temper (of the horse), one who is pure, one who removes the defects and takes the (good) qualities is always an expert in all acts (engaging the horses). One who has entered the riding ground holding the bridle should ride his steed either from his right or left. An excellent horse should not be whipped at once after mounting. Whipping causes fright and fear would produce confusion.
288.4: The rider should conduct (the horse) in a gallop in the morning holding the rein. (He should conduct the horse) slowly in the evening holding the rein but without handling it. (The following are the four political expedients): stroking is said to be conciliation, isolation (from the other steeds is) division, whipping with the whip and other things (is) punishment and biding time (is reckoned as) gift. The left fore-leg should be tied with the rein to the left hind-leg (of a horse) of mischievous habit. It should be ridden by holding the left rein. After having looked at a trusted horse and after having taken a tirm seat on the saddle, ( the horse) should be made to touch his leg with the face by holding (the rein). Such a (posture known as) lokana is beneficial.
288.5: A wise man should know the loss of consciousness and destruction for a horse and the fourth rule, namely, the mofana, is laid down. A horse whose leg does not touch the ground in a small circle, that foot should be restrained by means of mofana and vakkana. After striking on the side by kicking (the horse) that has distracted mind while one remain on the seat, the rein is drawn and held by the foot. It is known as grdhya-kanfaka- pOyanam. If a horse stands on the feet and hurts the rear legs, it is known as khalikdra (hurting).
288.6: The trot, the gallop or the canter. It would be ucchvasana (exhalation), if the horse is hurt and taken through a quadrangle by means of a different bridle by cheering. After restraining by any one of the three (ways) in order, it should be controlled by taking to the courses such as the circles and the like in order.
288.7: A wise man should relax and ride a horse that raises its head from its knee onwards. One should rise a horse till its limbs are light. The hinder leg should not be freed when (the horse) becomes quiet. Then it should be drawn forward with the hands by means of the bridle. The horse stands with the part about the hips becoming normal, the neck raised, and face on level. The cowdung, salt and (cow's) urine boiled with mud is besmeared on the body as a remedy for bites of flies, etc. The scum of boiled rice should be given by the rider to ( the horses) belonging to the bhadra and other breeds. The bites of tiny insects make the horse feel indolent and hungry.
288.8: A horse should be trained in such a way that it would become tamed. Horses would perish if they are made to run much. They do not get practice if not made to run. If the faces become white, (the horses) should be made to run. (Horses are said to be of four varieties such as bhadrOt manda mrga and sadkirna.) The (type of horse known as) bh(uira could be trained well, the manda variety, (by making use of ) a stick. (The type) of horse (known as) mrgdt. (is classified) taking the shank of a deer (as the basis). The above charac¬ teristics would be found mixed in the sadkirna class. The horse that eats sugar, honey, and fried rice and has a good aroma is said to be clean and belonging to the brahmin class. The horse that belongs to the warrior class would be lustrous, meek and clever. ( If the above qualities are found in lesser proportions it is known as the vaiiya cleiss.) (The horse that is) impure, unsteady, dull, ugly, foolish and wicked (is said to belong to) the Sudra (class).

289.1: The pairs of curls of hair on the skull, uparandhra (flanks), head, chest, forehead and neck of a horse are (deemed to be auspicious.
289.2: The curls of hair at the corner of the mouth, forehead, the root of the ear, the throat, root of the forelegs, neck arc auspicious. (The curls of hair) at other (places) are inauspi¬ cious.
289.3: The horses which resemble the colour of a parrot, indragopa (a kind of insect), moon and a crow and those which have a golden colour and are glossy are always commendable.
289.4: One should dismiss all the hopes of conquest where the horses of the kings have long necks, broad eye-corners and auspicious short ears.
289.5: Anointing with the roots of lodhra and karahjay mdlu-- lunga, agnU dried ginger, kustka, asafoetida, vaid and rdsnd would cure swelling.
289.6: Anointment with kafutaila of the affected parts (of a horse) is commended in the case of swelling in the wrist, cheek or throat or stiff-neck.
289.7: (A horse) that is affected by stiff-throat would have probably swelling in the region of the throat. A sternuta¬ tory with mustard, mhni rock-salt, juice of holy basil, black pepper and asafoetida (is given).
289.8: The five spices such as the long pepper, etc.
289.9: Clarified butter in the autumn and summer, oil in the cold and spring (seasons) and through the syringe in the advanced winter is desired to be the restraining (remedy).
289.10: Horses should be bathed and made to drink only once on the advent of the rains. On an extremely stormy day drinking only once is commended.
289.11: When heat and cold are blended in a season, (horses) should be made to drink twice and bathe once. In the summer they should be bathed and led to drink thrice and should be allowed to plunge (into the water) for a long time.

292.1: A king should protect cows and brahmins. I shall des¬ cribe the propitiation of cows. Cows are sacred and auspicious. The world is sustained by them.
292.2: Their feces and urine are the excellent destroyers of poverty. Stroking of a cow and the water from its horns would destroy multitudes of sins.
292.3: The urine and feces of a cow, milk, curd, clarified butter and rocani (yellow pigment got from a cow) are the six constituents that are excellent and when drunk they would prevent bad dreams etc.
292.4: (Go) rocan&is capable of nullifying poison and demons. One who feeds the cow with a morsel of food would go to heaven. In whose house cows are ill-kept, that person would go to hell.
292.5: One who gives a morsel of food to a cow belonging to another would go to heaven. One who does good to a cow would reach the world of Brahma. One who makes a gift of a cbw, one who sings her praise and one who saves her life would elevate his family. The earth becomes pure by the breath of cows. Sins get destroyed by their touch.
292.6: Obeisance to cows! To the fortunate ones! To the fragrant ones! Obeisance to the daughters of Brahma! Obeisance to the holy ones!

293.1: Listen to me! 1 shall describe the science relating to the mystic formulas that would yield enjoyment and emancipation. O Brahmin! The mystic formulas containing more than twenty letters are known to be maldmantra-s.
293.2: The mystic formulas having more than ten letters (and less than twenty) are designated as arvdgbija-s. These yield results in the old age, while the mdldmantras in the youth.
293.3: The formulas having more than five letters yield fruits always. The other formulas belonging to the group of mantras are of three kinds such as feminine, masculine and neuter. The feminine man/rof end -with (the term) Svaha (consort of Fire). The neuter mantras end with (the term) obeisance. The rest are masculine. They are commended (to be used) in charms to subjugate and' to drive away (evil). The feminine {mantras) (are used) to destroy diseases due to mean acts, while the neuter ones in other cases.
293.4: A mantra would not accomplish (the result) if it is either asleep or awakened. The sleeping state (of a mantra) is when there is powerful (breath through the nostrils and the waking state when the breath) flows through the right (nostril).

294.1: The different species of serpents, their nature, the ten places (in the body at which a bite would be fatal), the re¬ medial action, (the resultant) impurity and the behaviour of the (person) bitten (by the serpent) are said to be the seven characteristics.
294.2: The sex of the person bitten should be known as male or female or hermaphrodite from he flow of the breath forcibly through the left or right or both me nostrils of the self ( the snake-charmer) or the messenger.
294.3: One should indicate that part of the body as having been bitten which the messenger touches (when he meets the snake-charmer). It forebodes evil if the messenger moves his legs. If one has his (foot) raised without movement it indicates good.
294.4: If the messenger has an animal by his side (when conveying the news), it augurs good. If he is found with any¬ thing else it forebodes evil. If the animal that is present paces here and there, it forebodes bad. But (if it paces here and there) when the messenger is conveying (the message), it augurs good.
294.5: The presence of letters sacred to Wind and Fire (gods) at the beginning of a speech of the messenger is not good. (The presence of a letter sacred to) Hari (Indra) is mediocre. (The presence of) letters (sacred) to Varuna (god of water) is com¬ mendable. (The presence of) hermaphrodite (letters) is ex¬ tremely ominous.
294.6: An auspicious sentence (heard as the messenger) de¬ parts or the thundering of a cloud or the trumpeting of an elephant are auspicious. The circular movement (of birds) or crying from a fruit or tree on the left side is (also) auspicious.
294.7: Sounds such as music etc. would be auspicious. Such things would accomplish the result. Worthless words or words expressing a calamity, a wailing sound, a scream heard from the right (side), a sneezing (are bad omen).

311.1: I shall describe the (rite of) initiation etc. after having located in a lotus (diagram) furnished with (a diagram of) lion and thunderbolt. (The Tvarita-mezn/ra for this is): **He he, huti, Vajradanta ( one having the tooth like the thunder-bolt)! puru, purtty lulu, roar, roar here! Obeisance to the lion seat!" There should be four lines running across and vertical. A wise man should draw nine squares (formed by these lines). Only the squares in the directions should be taken and those in the in between directions should be destroyed. Outside the angular points of the chambers there should be eight outer lines. The outer line should be divided into two so that the middle horn of the vajra occupies the middle of the outside of the outer chamber. The outer line would be curved. A wise man should divide it into two. The central chamber would have a radiant lotus having yellow petals. One should draw the thunder-bolt and sword above (the lotus) with black dust. The outer square should be adorned with the sign of a thunder-bolt. The votary should add lour signs of thunder-bolt at the entrance. ( If it is done so) the centre of the lotus and the left line will be on the same line. The centre as well as the petals (should be made) red. Initiated women (should be worshipped) in this circle.
311.2: After striking with (the repetition of the mantra of) the weapon, the secret subordinate {mantras) should be located in the disciple. Tlie disciple should be bound with the subordinate {mantras) and then charged with the subordinate {mantras). Then the disciple should be made to throw a flower. He is then led to the sacrificial pit. One hundred oblations should be made with the principal mantra with barley, grains, sesamum and clarified butter. The first oblation (is intended for) the state of a plant, the next one for the state of reptiles (like the serpents), and (the subsequent oblations are) for the states of being a bird, animal and human beings, mortals, Brahma, Vi$nu and Rudra. 342.1: When the sun has not risen the votary should be bathed on a seat with ( the waters of ) pitchers (with the repetition of the following words): Orh obeisance to Lord Rudra ad to Bala besmeared with ashes of grey colour. Victory! Victory! Trample, down all the enemies of a weak man in wars and arguments. Orh! Crush down all the (hostile) marchers. Let that god who desires to barn (all the worlds) at the end of the yuga (period), and who having terrible form (accept) this worship. Let that god having thousand rays and white (in complextion) protect your life. May that (Lord) Siva, the destroyer of Tripura, who resembles the samvartaka fire and is of the form of all the gods, protect your life; likhi., likhi, khili oblations. After bathing, oblations should be done with scsa- mum and rice with (the repetition of the above) sacred formulas.
342.2: After having bathed with the pahcdmftaj the trident bearing lord should be worshipped. I sliall describe ( to you) the other kinds of ablutions that would always be for your victory.
342.3: (Bathing) with milk would be (giving) strong intellect and with curd, would further fortune. One would be destroying the sins by bathing with kuSa grass and would get all the things by bathing with the five things got from a cow.
342.4: One would get everything (by bathing) with Satamfila. One would destroy the sins (by bathing) with the waters (touched by) the horns of a cow. One would get everything by bathing with palaia bilvoy lotus and kuSa (grass).
342.5: The three cities of the demons T&rak&kfa, Kamal&ka and Vidyun- m&lin.
342.6: The fire that destroys the universe at the end.

342.8: One would gain health and excellent fortune respec¬ tively (by bathing) with water containing fruits and water with dhairi. One would get wealth and fortune respectively (by bathing) with sesamum and wiiite mustard.ind priyaAgu.
342.9: (One would gain) wealth (by bathing with water containing) lotus, blue lotus and kadamba. (One would gain) strength (by bathing) with the water containing (the twigs of) the bald tree. Bathing with the water that has washed the feet of (Lord) Visnu is the best among all kinds of ablutions.

359.1: Tlie characteristics of disease due to phlegm are languor, flow of water (from the mouth), heaviness (of the body), sweet taste in the mouth and longing for heat.
359.2: (Eating of) oil and hot food, anointing the body with oil and bathing and drinking of oil and the like would appease (deranged) wind. Clarified butter, milk, sugar and the rays of the moon and the like would counter (deranged) bile.
359.3: The oil of the three myrobalans together with honey and doing exercises etc. would remove (deranged) phlegm. Contemplation on (Lord) Visnu and His worship would appease all the diseases.
359.4: O One possessing powerful arms! The tastes such as sweet, sour and saline are stated to come from the moon. The tastes — bitter, astringent and pungent — arc (known to be) from fire.
359.5: The herbs have three flavours — bitter, sour and saline. The strength (of the herbs) is said to be of two kinds — hot and cold.
359.6: O Foremost among the brahmins! The effect of the herbs is indescribable. Those that are sweet, astringent and bitter are said to be having cold potency. The rest are stated to be hot.
359.7: The saline and sweet teistes would become sweet flavour. The sour things that are hot are also said to become so. The rest would have pungent flavour.
359.8: One has to determine the drugs that have got modified in their potency and flavour from their efficacy. Honey, although sweet, is said to be pungent in flavour.
359.9: (The herb) should be boiled with water, sixteen times its proportion, until it comes down to four times the proportion. This is the general rule for (preparing) a decoction wherever (something else) has not been stated.
359.10: The decoction that is clear and having little medicinal ingredient would be as above described. (The dosage) for pulverised drugs is stated to be an aka (a particular measure of weight equal to lrnAfas) and four palas (a particular weight) for the decoction. This measure is said to be middling. There is no hard and fast rule about the dosage. O Fortunate one! The measure of the dosage has to be decided according to the age, time, strength, digestive power, place, herb and disease.
359.11: One should eat the three myrobalans together with the rock-salt, that would give good complexion to a king. (One would get similar benefit by using) the juice of venison together with rock-salt or curd or small quantities of milk. One whose constitution is windy should eat (a food) that has either more juice or the same proportion of juice. It is said that massaging (the body) (should be done) in sum'mer. In winter it should be in equilibrium. It is known to be of middling type in the spring. The intense massaging in the summer is first done on the skin and then on the muscles, veins, blood and the body.

368.1: One who knows the means (of handling an emergent situation ), one who knows the temper (of the horse), one who is pure, one who removes the defects and takes the (good) qualities is always an expert in all acts (engaging the horses).
368.2: One who has entered the riding ground holding the bridle should ride his steed either from his right or left.
368.3: An excellent horse should not be whipped at once after mounting. Whipping causes fright and fear would produce confusion.
368.4: The rider should conduct (the horse) in a gallop in the morning holding the rein. (He should conduct the horse) slowly in the evening holding the rein but without handling it.
368.5: (The following are the four political expedients): stroking is said to be conciliation, isolation (from the other steeds is) division, whipping with the whip and other things (is) punishment and biding time (is reckoned as) gift.
368.6: The left fore-leg should be tied with the rein to the left hind-leg (of a horse) of mischievous habit. It should be ridden by holding the left rein.
368.7: After having looked at a trusted horse and after having taken a tirm seat on the saddle, ( the horse) should be made to touch his leg with the face by holding (the rein). Such a (posture known as) lokana is beneficial.
368.8: A wise man should know the loss of consciousness and destruction for a horse and the fourth rule, namely, the mofana, is laid down.
368.9: A horse whose leg does not touch the ground in a small circle, that foot should be restrained by means of mofana and vakkana.
368.10: After striking on the side by kicking (the horse) that has distracted mind while one remain on the seat, the rein is drawn and held by the foot. It is known as grdhya-kanfaka- pOyanam.
368.11: If a horse stands on the feet and hurts the rear legs, it is known as khalikdra (hurting).
368.12: The trot, the gallop or the canter.
368.13: It would be ucchvasana (exhalation), if the horse is hurt and taken through a quadrangle by means of a different bridle by cheering.

369.1: A wise man should relax and ride a horse that raises its head from its knee onwards. One should rise a horse till its limbs are light.
369.2: The hinder leg should not be freed when (the horse) becomes quiet. Then it should be drawn forward with the hands by means of the bridle. The horse stands with the part about the hips becoming normal, the neck raised, and face on level.
369.3: The cowdung, salt and (cow's) urine boiled with mud is besmeared on the body as a remedy for bites of flies, etc.
369.4: The scum of boiled rice should be given by the rider to ( the horses) belonging to the bhadra and other breeds. The bites of tiny insects make the horse feel indolent and hungry.
369.5: A horse should be trained in such a way that it would become tamed. Horses would perish if they are made to run much. They do not get practice if not made to run. If the faces become white, (the horses) should be made to run.
369.6: (Horses are said to be of four varieties such as bhadrOt manda mrga and sadkirna.) The (type of horse known as) bh(uira could be trained well, the manda variety, (by making use of ) a stick. (The type) of horse (known as) mrgdt. (is classified) taking the shank of a deer (as the basis). The above charac¬ teristics would be found mixed in the sadkirna class.
369.7: The horse that eats sugar, honey, and fried rice and has a good aroma is said to be clean and belonging to the brahmin class. The horse that belongs to the warrior class would be lustrous, meek and clever. ( If the above qualities are found in lesser proportions it is known as the vaiiya cleiss.) (The horse that is) impure, unsteady, dull, ugly, foolish and wicked (is said to belong to) the Sudra (class).
369.8: The pairs of curls of hair on the skull, uparandhra (flanks), head, chest, forehead and neck of a horse are (deemed to be auspicious.
369.9: The curls of hair at the corner of the mouth, forehead, the root of the ear, the throat, root of the forelegs, neck arc auspicious. (The curls of hair) at other (places) are inauspi¬ cious.
369.10: The horses which resemble the colour of a parrot, indragopa (a kind of insect), moon and a crow and those which have a golden colour and are glossy are always commendable.
369.11: One should dismiss all the hopes of conquest where the horses of the kings have long necks, broad eye-corners and auspicious short ears.

370.1: Anointment with kafutaila of the affected parts (of a horse) is commended in the case of swelling in the wrist, cheek or throat or stiff-neck.
370.2: (A horse) that is affected by stiff-throat would have probably swelling in the region of the throat. A sternuta¬ tory with mustard, mhni rock-salt, juice of holy basil, black pepper and asafoetida (is given).
370.3: The five spices such as the long pepper, etc.
370.4: Clarified butter in the autumn and summer, oil in the cold and spring (seasons) and through the syringe in the advanced winter is desired to be the restraining (remedy).
370.5: Horses should be bathed and made to drink only once on the advent of the rains. On an extremely stormy day drinking only once is commended.
370.6: When heat and cold are blended in a season, (horses) should be made to drink twice and bathe once. In the summer they should be bathed and led to drink thrice and should be allowed to plunge (into the water) for a long time.

374.1: One should begin the repetition of a mantra facing the east or looking downwards. All the mantras should begin with the pranava (the syllable Oih). One should restrain from convers¬ ing and eat the prescribed food.
374.2: One has to repeat the mantras remaining seated. He should look at his preceptor and the (favourite) deity alike. The places (suited for the practice) are a solitary cottage, temples and (banks of) rivers and tanks.
374.3: The fire-god, Dasra (Asvini devata), Uma (con¬ sort of Siva), Nighna (Vinayaka?), Naga (serpent), the Moon (Candra), the Sun, the divine mothers, (goddess) Durga, the presiding deities of the cardinal points, Krsna, Vaivasvata (god of death), Siva, the Moon (Sasanka) and the Pitrs are the presiding deities of the lunar days.
374.4: After having written (the names of) the Rudras together with their consorts at first, then ending with obeisance, they should be assigned in order. Then the aAga-mantras should be located. All the mantras with their constituents are capable of yielding perfection.
374.5: The different species of serpents, their nature, the ten places (in the body at which a bite would be fatal), the re¬ medial action, (the resultant) impurity and the behaviour of the (person) bitten (by the serpent) are said to be the seven characteristics.
374.6: The sex of the person bitten should be known as male or female or hermaphrodite from he flow of the breath forcibly through the left or right or both me nostrils of the self ( the snake-charmer) or the messenger.
374.7: One should indicate that part of the body as having been bitten which the messenger touches (when he meets the snake-charmer). It forebodes evil if the messenger moves his legs. If one has his (foot) raised without movement it indicates good.
374.8: If the messenger has an animal by his side (when conveying the news), it augurs good. If he is found with any¬ thing else it forebodes evil. If the animal that is present paces here and there, it forebodes bad. But (if it paces here and there) when the messenger is conveying (the message), it augurs good.
374.9: The presence of letters sacred to Wind and Fire (gods) at the beginning of a speech of the messenger is not good. (The presence of a letter sacred to) Hari (Indra) is mediocre. (The presence of) letters (sacred) to Varuna (god of water) is com¬ mendable. (The presence of) hermaphrodite (letters) is ex¬ tremely ominous.
374.10: An auspicious sentence (heard as the messenger) de¬ parts or the thundering of a cloud or the trumpeting of an elephant are auspicious. The circular movement (of birds) or crying from a fruit or tree on the left side is (also) auspicious.
374.11: Sounds such as music etc. would be auspicious. Such things would accomplish the result. Worthless words or words expressing a calamity, a wailing sound, a scream heard from the right (side), a sneezing (are bad omen).
